newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Dominguez bourse farce causes anger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Dominguez bourse farce causes anger.

text.p: An avalanche of orders to sell shares in fashion company Adolfo Dominguez on their second listed day swamped the Madrid bourse on Wednesday, forcing it to curb the trade which threatened to block the entire market.
Stock exchange officials were inundated with calls from irate investors wanting to sell their shares before the price fell further, sources said.
Dealers were snowed under by thousands of small sell orders after the shares in the prestigious fashion design company nearly doubled in price at Tuesday's debut.
There were so many tiny orders that the shares had to be negotiated via a system which involves matching them with buyers while the stock is not actively traded live on screen.
At 1500 GMT, the bourse decided to allow the stock to trade normally again, although a 15 percent trading fluctuation curb was in effect.

If the shares had been traded all day on the continuous market, operations on the entire bourse would have been slowed down because of the technical overspill amid a raft of orders, market sources said.
At 1600 GMT, the stock was traded at 5,060 pesetas, down 14.96 percent from Tuesday's close, on volume of 158,821 shares. Sell orders waiting were for 1.09 million shares.
On Tuesday it rose to 5,950 from a placement price of 3,100 pesetas for institutions and 3,007 pesetas for small investors.
This hugely successful flotation for up to 5.9 million shares was over-subscribed a record 112 times. Retail investors were allocated up to a paltry 15 shares.
For many, this factor would not make it worthwhile to hold onto the investment, especially when the stock doubled in value in just one day, dealers said.
"The flotation is a success because of the first price at which it was first quoted and the oversubscription, but you can't sell the shares," said a dealer who requested anonymity.
For the retail tranche, every shareholder was allocated three shares, plus roughly 0.36 percent of the number of shares they originally requested.
This means that there are plenty of orders in the market for four, five or up to 15 shares. For the whole morning's trade, accumulated sell orders totalled around one million shares.
Dealers too were none too pleased by today's events.
"There's no liquidity whatsoever in the stock and the electronic trading system won't support the volume of sales from small investors," said a dealer at an independent brokerage.
"If you want to sell, you have to stand in a queue and if you're lucky, it'll be your turn before it closes and that way your client won't lose another 15 percent," said one disgruntled trader.
